answer: The CIA records describe a Soviet citizen’s report from Site 7 at Sary Shagan on an evening in late summer 1973. The witness said they saw a bright green circular object or mass in the sky west of the site. Within 10 to 15 seconds, the circle widened and several green concentric circles formed; the color faded within minutes. The witness reported no accompanying sound and could not determine the object’s altitude or size. The supplied records do not identify what caused the phenomenon [UNDATED-CIA-6E72CA] [UNDATED-CIA-158652].

The archive records that Chief Petty Officer Delbert C. Newhouse took approximately 30 feet of handheld 16mm color film at 11:10 a.m. MST on July 2, 1952, about seven miles north of Tremonton, Utah. The record describes roughly 10–12 unidentified objects moving west in a loose formation, with one reversing course and filmed separately. The filming fragment is marked unresolved; it does not establish what the objects were [1952-USN-80203D].

A separate archive record describes Newhouse’s observation and says two photographs were taken, but that the objects appeared too small on film to show detail. That fragment is marked identified, without specifying an identification in the supplied evidence. The records therefore carry different resolution labels, and the evidence here does not explain why [1952-DOW-141453].
The December 12, 1948 green fireball was reported from two observation stations in New Mexico, near Starvation Peak (Bernal) and Los Alamos [1948-USAF-DDD5CA].

On November 19, 1968, USS Clyatt’s radar detected an unidentified object near Puerto Rico. The record says it appeared on radar for about 21 seconds and seemed to close on a fighter from the east to within a few miles. The fragment records no identification of the object. [1968-USN-6F2707]

The witnesses described a potato-shaped object with distinct edges and a creamy-white, opalescent appearance over the Cheyenne Mountains. They said it remained still for about two minutes before vanishing [UNDATED-USA-599D8B].
The witness reported lights forming a triangular pattern, with a light in the center—not a confirmed triangular-shaped object [UNDATED-FBI-380101].

The archive describes the “ghost rockets” as a wave of 1946 reports across Scandinavia, not one sighting. One account says the press first reported “flying missiles” over southern Sweden in late May and gave them the name. Reports followed from Finland and Denmark in June and Norway by July. Witnesses described a “ball of fire with a tail” or shiny cigar-shaped objects; Swedish authorities received nearly 1,000 reports through October [UNDATED-DOW-EA3896].

A separate archive account describes sightings in Swedish skies from February to December 1946, generally of elongated objects, sometimes resembling spheres or disks. Some reportedly left luminous trails or changed altitude suddenly [1946-NASA-A146CF].

The two fragments differ in their recorded resolutions: the first is marked “identified,” but the supplied evidence does not say what it was identified as; the second is marked “unresolved.” Neither establishes what caused the reports [UNDATED-DOW-EA3896] [1946-NASA-A146CF].

On the night of 19 November, the Crusader pilot reported seeing a delta-shaped object about the size of a jet fighter. The record says there was a full moon and good visibility, and estimates the object’s speed at more than Mach 3. The fragment remains unresolved [1968-USN-85858D].

On October 4, 1955, a U.S. tourist and three companions aboard a train roughly 50–65 miles south of Baku reported seeing a squat, equilateral-triangle-shaped object on an airfield about two miles away. The witness estimated it was about the size of a U.S. jet fighter and described a light at each corner. A searchlight illuminated the object; according to the report, it then launched, made roughly three to seven fast spirals, and climbed steeply at about a 45-degree angle while the searchlight tracked it. The supplied record lists the case as unresolved [1955-CIA-E34C6D].

The CIA material describes an unidentified, disc-like object hovering at high altitude over Harare International Airport on the afternoon of July 2, 2008. It was reported as possibly observed by both radar and optical means. The archive summary says it had rotating lights underneath, shifted colors, and then ascended quickly out of visual range. The fragment records the incident as unresolved [2008-CIA-052DE8].

The January 30, 1949 record describes a green fireball in the Socorro, New Mexico area. It says that air and ground searches were conducted in early February along its “well determined” ground track, but no fragments were recovered. The record lists the case as unresolved [1949-USAF-5C0132].

The archive has an FBI report dated October 1, 2023, describing a witness’s sighting near Colorado Springs. The witness said a dark-gray cloud dissipated as a large black triangular object emerged, with a red light at each corner. The witness reported that it initially moved at about helicopter speed, then appeared to accelerate and bank unusually before disappearing. The fragment is recorded as unresolved; the supplied evidence does not establish what the object was [2023-FBI-6A299C].

The Blue Book material reports a “seven inch ball of flame with eight foot trail” sighted from Phoenix at about 4:20 a.m. on July 2, 1952. It was reported to have moved in an arc from northwest to southwest over three to four minutes. The fragment records the sighting as unresolved [1952-USAF-0585D4].

On 24 November 1968, the Atlantic Fleet Weapons Range tracked an unidentified high-speed, high-altitude target near Puerto Rico. The record says it rapidly pulled away from a Crusader aircraft flying at Mach 0.99 at 45,000 feet; it does not identify the target [1968-USN-9E57C2].

The undated USAF record describes T-33 pilots chasing a reported large, disc-shaped object near Sandy Hook and Fort Monmouth. About ten minutes later, radar stations in the area reportedly picked up objects moving back and forth, with speeds described as reaching 3,500 mph. The archive marks the fragment “identified,” but the supplied evidence does not say what identification was made [UNDATED-USAF-58C451].
The agency or branch is **not stated** on the Sary Shagan fragments [UNDATED-CIA-6E72CA] [UNDATED-CIA-158652].
The USS Clyatt radar case is dated 1968 [1968-USN-6F2707].
The Tremonton filming fragment records the branch as USN (U.S. Navy) [1952-USN-80203D].
The Phoenix ball-of-flame fragment is recorded as **unresolved** [1952-USAF-0585D4].
The recorded location is between the train and the Caspian Sea coast in the Azerbaijan SSR, approximately 50–65 miles south of Baku [1955-CIA-E34C6D].
The recorded location text is “Cheyenne Mountains.” [UNDATED-USA-599D8B]
The December 20, 1948 Los Alamos green fireball fragment records the branch as USAF [1948-USAF-BFA2CC].
The Atlantic Fleet high-speed target fragment records the date as 24 November 1968 [1968-USN-9E57C2].
The ghost-rockets fragment records the location as southern Sweden, Finland, Denmark, and Norway [UNDATED-DOW-EA3896].
Yes. The October 2023 Colorado Springs triangular report lists “FBI” as its agency or branch in the fragment metadata [2023-FBI-6A299C].
The Western U.S. 2023 series represents **21 canonical events**, not one event. The supplied evidence lists multiple fragments for some of those events [UNDATED-FBI-FEDFE7] [UNDATED-FBI-2EAE94].

The supplied archive links the Colorado Springs 2022 event to three source files: FBI-UAP-D002.pdf as the primary narrative, FBI-UAP-D003.pdf as media for the event, and ICA-UAP-D001.pdf as analysis of the event. These are source relationships for one canonical event, not three separate sightings [UNDATED-USA-599D8B].

No. The archive lists FBI-UAP-D003.pdf as “media_for_event” for the Cheyenne Mountain observation, whose canonical event is Colorado Springs 2022. It is a rendering associated with that event, not a separate incident [UNDATED-USA-599D8B].

The archive does list a separate Colorado Springs observation from October 2023, but that is the black triangular object report, not the media rendering [2023-FBI-6A299C].

The archive lists ICA-UAP-D001.pdf as an analysis of the Colorado Springs 2022 event, but the supplied evidence contains none of that analysis’s findings or methods. It also lists FBI-UAP-D002.pdf as the primary narrative and FBI-UAP-D003.pdf as event media. The available fragment describes a reported observation over Cheyenne Mountain and records its resolution as unresolved; that is not, by itself, an analytical conclusion [UNDATED-USA-599D8B].

They describe the same place: Site 7 at Sary Shagan. Canada and the USSR appear because the witness was watching a televised sports competition, not because the sighting occurred in either country [UNDATED-CIA-6E72CA] [UNDATED-CIA-158652]. The archive lists the fragments under separate canonical events, although their descriptions are very similar; the supplied evidence does not establish whether they document the same occurrence.

The Tremonton material should be described as **one filming episode**, not several unrelated events. The supplied archive places the film in one canonical event: Newhouse filmed a group of roughly 10–12 objects, then tracked one object separately as it reversed course. That change in what he filmed does not make it a separate event. The fragment’s recorded resolution is unresolved [1952-USN-80203D].

The three records concern U.S. Navy reports from the vicinity of Puerto Rico in November 1968. Each describes an unidentified object in connection with a fighter aircraft, and each fragment is marked unresolved. They are recorded as three distinct events, not one: a USS Clyatt radar detection on November 19 [1968-USN-6F2707], a Crusader pilot’s visual observation that night [1968-USN-85858D], and an Atlantic Fleet Weapons Range track on November 24 [1968-USN-9E57C2].

The observations differ—radar detections versus a pilot’s visual account—and the supplied evidence does not establish what the objects were.

No. The records describe separate green-fireball observations on December 12 and December 20, 1948, and mark both fragments unresolved; neither identifies an aircraft as the fireball [1948-USAF-DDD5CA] [1948-USAF-BFA2CC]. The B-29 mentioned in a different record was the aircraft from which an observer watched a 1946 meteor shower, not an identification of the Los Alamos fireballs [1946-USAF-380402].

It describes a series of events, not one object seen once. The archive groups the Western US Event material as 21 canonical events. The reports include orange orbs said to have appeared at least five times over two days [UNDATED-OTHER-26A05E], as well as a “Dark Kite” sighting and a kite-shaped object observed about 30 minutes later nearby [UNDATED-OTHER-FC97CA] [UNDATED-OTHER-E3736E]. These are reported observations; the supplied evidence does not establish what the objects were or whether any sightings involved the same physical object.

The **2022 Cheyenne Mountain narrative** is the account of a former Army intelligence officer and four unit members who reported a creamy-white, potato-shaped object over Cheyenne Mountain. Its fragment is dated *undated*, but the archive places it in the “Colorado Springs 2022” canonical event. FBI-UAP-D002.pdf is the primary narrative; FBI-UAP-D003.pdf is media for the same event, not a separate incident. The fragment’s resolution is recorded as unresolved [UNDATED-USA-599D8B].

The **October 2023 triangular report** is a separate Colorado Springs event. A witness reported a black triangular object with red lights at its corners emerging from a cloud and later accelerating and banking. Its primary narrative is FBI-UAP-D030.pdf, and its fragment is also recorded as unresolved [2023-FBI-6A299C].

The supplied Tremonton records leave the assessment unclear. The filming fragment records Newhouse’s observation of objects he could not identify and is marked unresolved [1952-USN-80203D]. A separate Tremonton fragment is marked identified, but its supplied account does not say what the objects were; it says they appeared too small on film to show detail [1952-DOW-141453]. The evidence does not explain how those differing recorded resolutions were reached or reconciled.

Yes. Both reports concern the vicinity of Puerto Rico on 19 November 1968: the Crusader pilot reported a visual observation that night, while the USS Clyatt reported a radar detection [1968-USN-85858D] [1968-USN-6F2707]. The archive lists them as separate canonical events, so the supplied evidence establishes the same date and area, not that they were the same encounter.

For the Colorado Springs 2022 event, FBI-UAP-D002.pdf is listed as the primary narrative, and FBI-UAP-D003.pdf is listed as media for that same event. They are related sources for one canonical event, not separate incidents [UNDATED-USA-599D8B]. The supplied evidence does not describe what the media file contains.

No. The December 12, 1948 record names observation stations near Starvation Peak (Bernal, New Mexico) and at Los Alamos; it describes one fireball observed from both places, not two separate events [1948-USAF-DDD5CA]. The separate December 20 record lists Los Alamos as its location [1948-USAF-BFA2CC].

No. The archive lists the October 2023 Colorado law-enforcement video and the Cheyenne Mountain narrative as separate fragments in separate canonical events. The video is a 1-minute, 19-second recording by a Colorado law-enforcement officer [UNDATED-LLE-A4576B]. The Cheyenne Mountain narrative describes an observation by a former Army intelligence officer and four unit members; the archive associates it with the Colorado Springs 2022 event [UNDATED-USA-599D8B].

The files describe a series of reported green or greenish-blue fireballs, particularly around New Mexico, but they do not give them all one explanation. A USAF account in DOW-UAP-D154.pdf says reports near Los Alamos described brilliant greenish-blue objects that resembled meteors but appeared to follow flat trajectories and not explode; that fragment is unresolved [UNDATED-USAF-B32231].

Two dated 1949 reports in DOW-UAP-D017.pdf concern the Socorro area. One records a fireball reported at 8:26 p.m. on July 24 and says airborne material was collected in an attempt to recover associated particles; the supplied evidence gives no result from that collection [1949-USAF-9D1046]. The other says air and ground searches along the January 30 fireball’s estimated ground track recovered no fragments [1949-USAF-5C0132].

The undated discussion in DOE-UAP-D004.pdf adds observations and comparisons, but the evidence does not establish that all of them belong to 1949. It contrasts a green fireball’s horizontal path with December 12 Geminid meteors and mentions an exceptionally bright fireball from the Geminid direction roughly an hour to an hour and a half later [UNDATED-DOE-80EBE8] [UNDATED-DOE-BBFEBB]. It also discusses a bright January 30 Texas fireball; the speaker explicitly says they did not see it and estimated its brightness from others’ comparisons with the moon. The supplied evidence does not establish that this was the January 30 Socorro-area report [UNDATED-DOE-5FC004] [1949-USAF-5C0132]. Another account says an object looked bronze from Kirtland Field but green from Arizona, where it reportedly turned straight down [UNDATED-USAF-6A96A7].

Finally, the same DOE file records a caution against treating every green sighting as unusual: one doubly observed yellow-green fireball was estimated to descend from about 199 to 100 kilometers and was assessed as an ordinary fireball [UNDATED-DOE-DA531C]. The other cited fragments remain unresolved in the supplied evidence; they report observations and searches, not an established cause.

The supplied archive evidence has two Tremonton records, but it does not explicitly identify either as Project Blue Book material.

One records Chief Petty Officer Delbert C. Newhouse filming about 30 feet of 16mm color film on July 2, 1952, seven miles north of Tremonton. It describes roughly 10–12 objects moving in a loose group and one that reversed course; the fragment’s resolution is listed as unresolved [1952-USN-80203D]. The other describes Newhouse’s observation at the same time and general location and says two photographs were taken, but the objects were too small on film to show detail. Its resolution is listed as identified, without an identification given in the supplied evidence [1952-DOW-141453].

The archive lists three unresolved U.S. Navy records from the vicinity of Puerto Rico in November 1968:

- On November 19, USS Clyatt detected an unidentified radar object for about 21 seconds; the record says it closed on a fighter from the east to within a few miles [1968-USN-6F2707].
- Also on the night of November 19, a Crusader pilot reported seeing a delta-shaped object about the size of a jet fighter in clear, full-moon conditions. Its speed was estimated at over Mach 3 [1968-USN-85858D].
- On November 24, the Atlantic Fleet Weapons Range tracked a high-speed, high-altitude target that reportedly pulled rapidly away from a Crusader flying at Mach 0.99 and 45,000 feet [1968-USN-9E57C2].

The archive treats these as three separate canonical events. None of the supplied records identifies the objects conclusively.

The supplied FBI-file excerpts do not mention Newark, so they do not establish what the files say about it. The New Jersey reports shown concern other locations, including Glen Ridge, Union, Woodbridge, and West Orange [1957-FBI-DB9934] [1958-FBI-B518F9] [1958-FBI-420E8E] [1958-FBI-D3842E].

The 1952 Utah film case represented is the Tremonton filming. On July 2, Chief Petty Officer Delbert C. Newhouse took approximately 30 feet of 16mm color motion-picture film seven miles north of Tremonton. The record describes 10–12 unidentified objects milling in a rough formation, with one object reversing course and tracked separately on film. The filming fragment is marked unresolved [1952-USN-80203D]. A separate Tremonton record from the same date is marked identified, but the supplied evidence does not explain that assessment [1952-DOW-141453].

The supplied evidence points to four radar or radar/sensor cases:

- At St. Louis, a B-29 radar-scoring operator reportedly saw a return at 48,000 feet descend toward the aircraft at an estimated 1,000 mph. The account says the operator initially considered a possible radar harmonic; the case remains unresolved. The account appears in DOW-UAP-D154.pdf [UNDATED-USAF-5C92A2].
- At “New Spain Library,” a GCA operator reportedly tracked two returns approaching an incoming C-47. According to the account, the returns turned just after a tower warning broadcast. This unresolved account also appears in DOW-UAP-D154.pdf [UNDATED-USAF-539CFA].
- Near Japan, a pilot reported tracking objects on a radar/sensor display, with three visible at once. The fragment is dated August 31, 2020, and remains unresolved; it appears in DOW-UAP-D042.pdf [2020-USAF-82CB61].
- At France’s Cinq-Mars-la-Pile Control and Detection Center, a radar track was reportedly detected and recorded on January 28, 1994. The fragment does not identify what produced it and is marked unresolved [1994-USAF-3880AD].

These are reported observations and tracks, not established identifications of the objects involved.

The supplied material includes one green-fireball report in a DOE-labeled source file, DOE-UAP-D004.pdf: an undated account of a “remarkable” August 4 fireball near Oregon, noted as close in timing to a meteor shower. The fragment does not state an investigating agency or a resolved explanation [UNDATED-DOE-A60A48].

For the Los Alamos area, DOW-UAP-D017.pdf records two distinct December 1948 observations. A December 12 greenish-yellow fireball was observed from two New Mexico stations on a nearly horizontal path near Starvation Peak and Los Alamos [1948-USAF-DDD5CA]. On December 20, Los Alamos AESS inspectors observed a greenish-white fireball that reportedly descended and then followed a nearly horizontal path [1948-USAF-BFA2CC]. Both fragments are labeled USAF and unresolved.

Other supplied USAF material discusses reports of greenish-blue fireballs near Los Alamos and Albuquerque, including their reported flat trajectories and lack of explosion; it is an undated discussion of reports, not a newly dated sighting [UNDATED-USAF-B32231]. The same DOW file also contains separate 1949 green-fireball reports near Socorro, including an airborne-material collection effort after the July report and an unsuccessful search for fragments after the January report [1949-USAF-9D1046] [1949-USAF-5C0132].

The archive also lists reports of puzzling lights above Los Alamos atomic-energy laboratories and a white circular object seen from Santa Fe while a witness watched a plane land at Los Alamos. Neither is described in the supplied evidence as a green fireball [UNDATED-USAF-654FA5] [1948-DEPARTMENT-85544F].

The archive lists two separate Colorado local law-enforcement video records from October 2023:

- A law-enforcement officer recorded a 1-minute, 19-second video. Its transcript is in LLE-UAP-D001.pdf; AARO removed the audio to protect privacy and sensitive information. The record marks the UAP unresolved [UNDATED-LLE-A4576B].
- A law-enforcement officer recorded a 27-second video. Its transcript is in LLE-UAP-D003.pdf; the recording had indistinct background noise but no discernible dialogue. This record is also marked unresolved [UNDATED-LLE-2234ED].

The archive includes a CIA range report in CIA-UAP-011.pdf describing an observation at Site 7 of the Sary Shagan weapons testing range in late summer 1973. A Soviet citizen reported seeing a bright green circular object west of the site that expanded into concentric circles and faded, with no associated sound. The archive lists the sighting as unresolved; it does not establish what the object was. The case fragment itself is dated “undated,” while the account places the observation in 1973 [UNDATED-CIA-158652].

The released accounts describe a 1946 *wave of reports*, not one ghost-rocket incident. One account says the Swedish press first reported “flying missiles” over southern Sweden in late May and named them “Ghost Rockets.” Reports extended to Finland and Denmark in June and Norway by July; Swedish authorities received nearly 1,000 reports by October. The reported objects were described as “a ball of fire with a tail” or shiny, cigar-shaped objects [UNDATED-DOW-EA3896].

A separate account gives a broader February–December span for sightings in Swedish skies. It describes generally spindle-shaped objects, sometimes appearing spherical or disk-shaped, often moving horizontally, sometimes leaving a luminous trail, and reportedly able to ascend or descend suddenly. It says the sightings concerned military authorities in several Scandinavian countries [1946-NASA-A146CF].

The supplied excerpts do not establish what the reported objects were. Although one fragment is marked “identified,” the evidence here does not give an identification; the other is marked unresolved [UNDATED-DOW-EA3896] [1946-NASA-A146CF].

No. These records describe observations that remained unresolved or had insufficient data; neither finding establishes an extraterrestrial origin. For example, searches found no fragments from a 1949 green fireball, and a separate light observation was recorded as having insufficient data [1949-USAF-5C0132] [1949-USA-E98687].

The Mexican Congress record reports that presenters displayed **alleged** alien corpses and discussed a proposed law acknowledging alien life. It does not establish that the remains were alien or that extraterrestrials visited Earth [2023-DEPARTMENT-98C959].
None. The supplied records describe reported objects and lights, but no alien beings or species [UNDATED-USA-599D8B] [UNDATED-FBI-DA1DE3] [UNDATED-CIA-FDA367].

None of the supplied archive evidence establishes that any UAP definitely used anti-gravity. The records describe observations—including a steep launch near Baku and a high-speed target near Puerto Rico—but do not determine how those objects moved [1955-CIA-E34C6D] [1968-USN-9E57C2].

None of the supplied documents proves that alien bodies were recovered. The closest is an FBI record of a secondhand claim: an auto dealer relayed what an engineer named Coulter said he had seen at a radar station, including purported non-human remains. The archive marks that claim unresolved; recording it is not verification [UNDATED-FBI-AC2C].

If you mean the Gemini 5 spacecraft, the record names astronauts Cooper and Conrad, but does not say which one piloted it. It does not identify anyone piloting the object they observed [UNDATED-USN-35D21A].

None of the supplied cases conclusively proves non-human technology. The strongest-sounding recovery accounts are reported claims: Coulter was said to have seen recovered saucers and non-human remains [UNDATED-FBI-AC2C], while the Roswell account attributes an extraterrestrial-vessel claim to Colonel Corso [1947-USAF-A120D8]. Both fragments are recorded as unresolved, not as verified findings.

The supplied archive evidence does not identify or describe a secret treaty with an alien government. It includes a reported claim about recovered “flying saucers” [UNDATED-FBI-AC2C] and a Mexican congressional hearing where alleged alien remains were presented [2023-DEPARTMENT-98C959], but neither record establishes a treaty.

None. The supplied archive evidence does not confirm a weaponized UFO. One witness described an unidentified object as *resembling* an underwater demolition bomb, but the record does not say it was a weapon, and the sighting remained unresolved [1957-USAF-861A2D].

The supplied records do not locate or name an extraterrestrial base. “Sandia Base” is the location of a reported light observation, not an extraterrestrial base [1949-USA-E98687]. The Roswell record recounts Colonel Corso’s claim about an extraterrestrial vessel, but it does not identify a base [1947-USAF-A120D8].

None of the supplied incidents proves a crash retrieval of a flying saucer. The Roswell record says the base initially announced that personnel had recovered debris from a “flying disk,” but that statement was retracted and the object was described as a weather balloon [1947-USAF-2C9F14]. A separate FBI record contains a secondhand claim about recovered saucers, not a verified recovery [UNDATED-FBI-AC2C].
